The first time I noticed time behaving strangely was on a rainy afternoon, when the world seemed to move at half-speed. I remember watching a streetlight through a window streaked with water, the bulb glowing like something half-remembered. Cars hissed past on wet pavement, and every sound arrived a fraction late, as if it had to travel through a thicker air than usual. I couldn’t explain it. I only knew that the minutes felt padded, softer at the edges, like they were willing to be held.

Later, I tried to name the feeling: relief, maybe. Or curiosity. Or the quiet kind of attention you give a living thing when you don’t want to frighten it away. Because that’s what it was, I think—an invitation to notice.

I began paying attention the way people do when they’re trying to remember something important. I listened for small details: the click of a tap turning on, the muted conversation of neighbors, the occasional flutter of birds escaping from a tree that hadn’t fully decided whether it was spring. I realized that time wasn’t actually slowing; I was simply more awake.

There’s a myth that life is made of grand events, but most of it is built from ordinary seconds stacked carefully together. On that rainy afternoon, I felt the structure being assembled in real time. And for once, I didn’t rush to the next thing. I let the moment finish its sentence.
